Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For prime $e=p$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]; the same inequalities define the
extension to composite finite $e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $F$ be a field, $A$ a finite-dimensional cellular $F$-algebra with cellular
basis $(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$,
$D^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]],
[[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).
For $\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda$ with $D^{\mu}\ne0$ let
$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[C^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]$ be the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ as a
composition factor of $C^{\lambda}$ (well defined by
[[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] and
[[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\unrhd\mu,$$
i.e. a nonzero off-diagonal entry can occur only in the allowed direction of the
cell order $\unrhd$ (larger cell first). Order the labels by a linear extension from smaller to larger. The square
submatrix whose rows and columns both have nonzero $D$ is lower
unitriangular; the full rectangular matrix has the same labelled diagonal
and the stated vanishing region. This
determines only the diagonal and the vanishing region: no off-diagonal entry is
computed by cellularity.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$q$-integer** is

$$[n]_q := 1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1},$$

with $[0]_q:=0$.

The **$q$-factorial** is

$$[n]_q! := \prod_{i=1}^{n}[i]_q,$$

so $[0]_q!:=1$.

If $k_1,\dots,k_r \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $k_1+\cdots+k_r=n$, the
**$q$-multinomial coefficient** is

$$\binom{n}{k_1,\dots,k_r}_q := \frac{[n]_q!}{[k_1]_q!\cdots[k_r]_q!}.$$

These are polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$ once the integrality theorems of the
page are proved; at this point they are formal expressions to be identified by
their counting roles.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field. Its **Jacobson radical**
is

$$ J(A):=\bigcap\{L<A:L\text{ is a maximal left ideal of }A\}. $$

When $A\ne0$, maximal proper left ideals exist without a choice principle:
the proper left ideal $0$ exists, and among dimensions of proper left ideals
choose the largest integer. An ideal of that dimension is maximal because
strict containment strictly increases vector-space dimension. On
finite-dimensional algebras $J(A)$ is two-sided: for each simple left
$A$-module $S$ and each $0\ne s\in S$, the kernel of the surjection
$A\to S$, $a\mapsto as$, is a maximal left ideal. Hence an element in
every maximal left ideal annihilates every simple left module. Conversely,
an element annihilating every simple left module lies in each maximal left
ideal by applying it to $A/L$ and $1+L$. Thus $J(A)$ is the intersection of
the two-sided annihilators of all simple left modules, so $A/J(A)$ is an
algebra. This radical agrees with the usual right-sided definition.

derivations.claim: Use finite joint-primary projections without presupposing which labels survive. The regular right module has a cellular filtration with quotients copies of the cells; refining their common flags in [F3] gives a simultaneous triangular flag on it. Thus each $L_a$ is annihilated by a polynomial $\prod_b(X-b)^N$, with finitely many diagonal values $b\in F$ and $N\ge\dim H$. Polynomial Bezout and the Chinese remainder construction give $p_{a,b}$ congruent to one modulo $(X-b)^N$ and zero modulo the other factors. Substituting $L_a$ gives commuting idempotents. For a joint word $\xi$, their product $P_\xi$ is idempotent in $H$ and on a cell flag has diagonal one exactly at tableaux with word $\xi$, zero elsewhere. An idempotent has zero image if and only if all these diagonal entries vanish: its triangular matrix would otherwise be nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. The vector-space functor $M\mapsto MP_\xi$ is exact on $H$-modules, because a lift $x$ of $y=yP_\xi$ can be replaced by $xP_\xi$, and kernels are preserved. No centrality or $H$-submodule assertion for this image is needed.

For finite $e$, equality of two diagonal values $[a]_q,[b]_q$ is equivalent to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Indeed $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ for all integers, including negative integers. When $q\ne1$, $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$, and when $q=1$, $e=\operatorname{char}F$ and the q-integer is the integer reduced to $F$. Thus a joint word is exactly a residue word in the node convention $c-r\pmod e$.

Prove the complete ladder-boundary comparison. Put $L(s,c)=(e-1)s+c-e$. Suppose $\alpha$ is restricted, every occupied node has $L<l$, and the addable ladder-$l$ set is nonempty. Set $C=l+e-1$, $T=\lfloor C/(e-1)\rfloor$, $d=C-(e-1)T\in\{0,\ldots,e-2\}$ and $u_s=C-(e-1)s$. For $1\le s\le T$, $0\le\alpha_s\le u_s$, and no positive row occurs beyond $T$. The deficits $h_s=u_s-\alpha_s$ are nonnegative and satisfy $h_{s+1}-h_s=\alpha_s-\alpha_{s+1}-(e-1)\le0$. An addable ladder-$l$ row has deficit zero; thereafter every deficit is zero. Consecutive such rows have width difference $e-1>0$, so the ladder addables form a terminal interval $s_0,\ldots,T$. A first equality row that is not addable simply precedes this interval. Adding its bottommost $k$ nodes therefore adds in rows $T-k+1,\ldots,T$. The length of $\alpha$ is $T$ for $d>0$ and $T-1$ for $d=0$, including the empty case $T=1,d=0$. If $\beta\unrhd\alpha$ has the same size, its length is at most that of $\alpha$, by the prefix inequality at that length. For $d=0$ all addable rows of $\beta$ are at most $T$. For $d>0$ the sole possible extra row is $T+1$, with residue $-T$, different from $i=l\bmod e=d+1-T\bmod e$ since $1\le d+1<e$. Hence every addable $i$-node of $\beta$ lies in a row at most $T$. If $\gamma$ adds any $k$ of these initial addables, at row cutoff $r$ its prefix increment is at least $\max(0,k-\max(T-r,0))$, exactly the increment for the bottommost-$k$ extension $\delta$ of $\alpha$. Adding $\beta$'s prefix inequalities proves $\gamma\unrhd\delta$. This holds for every $k$ simultaneously and needs no same-content premise.

u T_a$. No scalar is divided out. Sorting $

Canonical-row support without factorial cancellation. The semistandard permutation-basis theorem [[lem-type-a-hecke-permutation-modules-have-semistandard-murphy-bases-and-specht-filtrations]], followed by star, gives an exact coordinate condition for $Hx_\rho$: every supported right Murphy tableau has semistandard type $\rho$. Apply it to the factor remaining after $[\beta]!_Q$ in step 1.4, before putting back $T_a$. This factor belongs to $Hx_\nu$. In shape $\eta$, semistandardness forces the first $\eta_1$ labels into the first row, the next $\eta_2$ into the second, and so on through $B$: a label cannot occur below its own row, and each earlier row is already full. Thus its right tableaux have the first $j$ canonical rows. The permutation $a$ uses only later labels. Expanding $T_a$ by the row action and straightening cannot alter these canonical rows: their prefix counts are maximal, and same-shape straightening increases every tableau-prefix count by that supplier's Statement. This proves the canonical-row assertion even for the quotient by the displayed factorial. Starting at $j=1$, repeat steps 1.4 and 2.1 for each surviving standard-tableau term. If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$, every surviving term at that stage has $\beta_j\ge e$, so $[e]!_Q$ divides its factor $[\beta]!_Q$. Later multiplication and integral straightening preserve this common divisor. This establishes the full repeated-symmetrizer support and divisibility used below.

For restricted $\eta$, number its nodes by increasing $L$, taking lower rows first on a tie, to obtain $t_\eta$. Moving right increases $L$ by one and moving down by $e-1$, so it is standard. The diagrams $\alpha_l$ of nodes with $L<l$ and $\delta_l$ with $L\le l$ are restricted: their row widths are the minimum of the restricted widths of $\eta$ and the positive part of the affine cutoff bound, each having adjacent difference at most $e-1$. A node on ladder $l$ forces every lower positive position on that ladder to be occupied, since $\eta_{s+1}\ge\eta_s-(e-1)$. Thus $\delta_l$ adds the bottommost $a_l$ ladder addables to $\alpha_l$. Any competing standard tableau with the same full residue word has, in the corresponding block, $a_l$ additions all of residue $l$. ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,

[[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\unrhd\mu,$$

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).

the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-.definition_or_statement_exact:
Let $F=\mathbb Q(q)$ with $q$ an indeterminate, let $N\ge1$, and put $K_i=L_iL_{i+1}^{-1}$ for $1\le i<N$. Start with the free associative $F$-algebra on $L_j,L_j^{-1}$ ($1\le j\le N$) and $E_i,F_i$ ($1\le i<N$), and quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by the following relations:

1. $L_jL_j^{-1}=L_j^{-1}L_j=1$ and $L_jL_k=L_kL_j$ for all $j,k$.
2. $L_jE_iL_j^{-1}=q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}E_i$ and $L_jF_iL_j^{-1}=q^{-\delta_{j,i}+\delta_{j,i+1}}F_i$.
3. $[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$.
4. $[E_i,E_j]=[F_i,F_j]=0$ when $|i-j|>1$.
5. For $|i-j|=1$, $E_i^2E_j-(q+q^{-1})E_iE_jE_i+E_jE_i^2=0$ and $F_i^2F_j-(q+q^{-1})F_iF_jF_i+F_jF_i^2=0$.

Here $[x,y]=xy-yx$. The free algebra and quotient construction are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]; this definition asserts existence of the presented associative algebra, not the well-definedness of structural maps on its quotient.

On $V_N$ with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$, prescribe the candidate matrices
$$L_je_a=q^{\delta_{ja}}e_a,\qquad E_ie_a=\delta_{a,i+1}e_i,\qquad F_ie_a=\delta_{a,i}e_{i+1}.$$
Prescribe candidate coproduct and counit values by
$$\Delta(L_j)=L_j\otimes L_j,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i,$$
and $\epsilon(L_j^{\pm1})=1$, $\epsilon(E_i)=\epsilon(F_i)=0$. The following relation-descent lemma proves that these assignments define the vector representation and bialgebra structure, and hence the tensor actions used below.

**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, $N\ge1$, the algebra presentation and candidate maps in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]].

[F1] A free associative algebra modulo the two-sided ideal of its displayed relations is a presented algebra, and assignments descend exactly when they annihilate every defining relation ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]).

[F2] The tensor product of algebras has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$, and maps agreeing on the displayed generators agree on the presented algebra ([[thm-tensor-product-of-algebras-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[lem-hh-universal-presentations-and-base-change]]).

[F3] For $a_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{i+1,j}$, the defining $L$-weight relations imply $K_iE_jK_i^{-1}=q^{a_{ij}}E_j$ and $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q^{-a_{ij}}F_j$; in particular $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$, $a_{ii}=2$, and $a_{ij}=-1$ for adjacent indices.
lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-a.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 On $V_N$, each $L_j$ is diagonal and invertible, and the $L_j$ commute. Conjugating the matrix unit $E_i:e_{i+1}\mapsto e_i$ by $L_j$ multiplies its sole nonzero entry by $q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}$; conjugating $F_i:e_i\mapsto e_{i+1}$ gives the inverse exponent. Also $K_i$ has eigenvalue $q$ on $e_i$, $q^{-1}$ on $e_{i+1}$ and $1$ on every other basis vector, so $(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $1,-1,0$ in those positions. Directly, $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $[E_i,F_i]$ is that diagonal matrix. Products $E_iE_j$ and $E_jE_i$ (and the corresponding $F$ products) both vanish when $|i-j|>1$; $E_i^2=F_i^2=0$, and each middle three-letter Serre product also vanishes because its matrix-unit indices do not compose. Thus every defining relation holds, and the quotient universal property [F1] gives the vector representation. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Define $\Delta$ on the free generators by the displayed formulas in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]]. The $\Delta(L_j)$ are mutually commuting units with the displayed inverses. Conjugation by $\Delta(L_j)$ gives the required weights on each of the two terms of $\Delta(E_i)$ and $\Delta(F_i)$, since each $K_i$ is a Laurent monomial in the commuting $L$'s. For any $i,j$, expansion gives $[\Delta(E_i),\Delta(F_j)]=[E_i,F_j]\otimes K_i+K_j^{-1}\otimes[E_i,F_j]+[E_i\otimes K_i,K_j^{-1}\otimes F_j]$. The last cross term is zero: its first product can be reordered as $q^{a_{ji}-a_{ij}}K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i=K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i$, which is its reverse product by [F3]. If $i\ne j$, the remaining terms vanish; if $i=j$, they sum to $\bigl(K_i\otimes K_i-K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\bigr)/(q-q^{-1})=\Delta\bigl((K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})\bigr)$. For $|i-j|>1$, $a_{ij}=0$ and the $K_i$ commute with $E_j,F_j$; expanding the two commutators therefore proves that the distant $E$ and $F$ relations are preserved. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $\gamma=q+q^{-1}$ and $S_{ij}(X,Y)=X^2Y-\gamma XYX+YX^2$ for adjacent $i,j$. For the $E$ relation write $\Delta(E_s)=A_s+B_s$ with $A_s=E_s\otimes K_s$, $B_s=1\otimes E_s$. In each of the three words $iij,iji,jii$, choose an $A$ at each selected position and a $B$ at each other position, then move the selected $K$ factors to the right using $K_rE_s=q^{a_{rs}}E_sK_r$. Grouping the resulting 24 terms by the number of selected positions gives: degree $0$ in the first factor is $1\otimes S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)$; degree $3$ is $S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)\otimes K_i^2K_j$; degree $1$ has respective coefficients $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $1+q^{-2}-\gamma q^{-1}$ on $E_i\otimes E_iE_jK_i$, $E_i\otimes E_jE_iK_i$, $E_j\otimes E_i^2K_j$; degree $2$ has respective coefficients $q^{-2}+1-\gamma q^{-1}$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$ on $E_i^2\otimes E_jK_i^2$, $E_iE_j\otimes E_iK_iK_j$, $E_jE_i\otimes E_iK_jK_i$. All six mixed coefficients are zero by the definition of $\gamma$, and the two pure terms vanish by the defining Serre relation. Thus $\Delta$ preserves every positive Serre relation. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The assignment $\phi(L_j)=L_j^{-1}$, $\phi(E_i)=F_i$, $\phi(F_i)=E_i$ preserves the presentation: it exchanges the two weight relations, sends the mixed commutator to its negative with $K_i$ replaced by $K_i^{-1}$, and exchanges the distant and Serre relations. It is an involution. On generators $\Delta(F_i)=\tau(\phi\otimes\phi)\Delta(E_i)$, where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is an algebra isomorphism. Since step 1.3 proves that the positive Serre polynomial maps to zero, applying the algebra maps $\tau$ and $\phi\otimes\phi$ proves that the negative Serre polynomial maps to zero as well. Together steps 1.2–2.1 show every relation is killed, so [F1] descends $\Delta$ to the quotient. The counit assignment kills the relations directly: each relation becomes either $1=1$ or $0=0$, so it too descends. [given, F1, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Both counit composites and both iterated coproduct composites are algebra homomorphisms, so it suffices by [F2] to check generators. The maps $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$ return $L_j,E_i,F_i$ from their displayed formulas. On $L_j$, both iterated coproducts give $L_j\otimes L_j\otimes L_j$; on $E_i$, both give $E_i\otimes K_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes1\otimes E_i$; on $F_i$, both give $F_i\otimes1\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i$. Hence $\Delta$ is coassociative with counit $\epsilon$. The vector representation of step 1.1 and the iterated coproduct therefore define actions on every $V_N^{\otimes n}$. They are finite sums and products of matrices with entries $0,1,q^{\pm1}$, so all entries lie in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S$ a set. There is a unital associative $R$-algebra $R\langle S\rangle$, the **free associative $R$-algebra on $S$**, whose underlying $R$-module is free on the set of finite words in $S$ (including the empty word), with product given on words by concatenation and extended $R$-bilinearly.

1. **Universal property.** For every $R$-algebra $A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and every map $S\to A$ there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $R\langle S\rangle\to A$ extending it. When $R=k$ is a field and $S$ indexes a basis of a vector space $V$, $R\langle S\rangle$ reproduces the published tensor algebra $T(V)$ ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]], [[thm-universal-property-of-the-tensor-algebra]]).
2. **Two-sided ideal description.** For $E\subseteq R\langle S\rangle$ the two-sided ideal $(E)$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) is the set of finite sums $\sum_sa_se_sb_s$ with $a_s,b_s\in R\langle S\rangle$ and $e_s\in E$.
3. **Quotient universal property.** If $\varphi:R\langle S\rangle\to A$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism killing $E$, then $\varphi$ factors uniquely through the quotient $R\langle S\rangle/(E)$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]); the quotient is the presented $R$-algebra with generators $S$ and relations $E$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A,B$ be $R$-algebras. The $R$-module $A\otimes_RB$ has a unique $R$-algebra structure satisfying

$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$$

and

$$1_{A\otimes_RB}=1_A\otimes1_B,\qquad r\longmapsto r(1_A\otimes1_B).$$

If $A$ and $B$ are commutative, then $A\otimes_RB$ is commutative.

Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, let $X$ be a set and let $R\langle X\rangle$ be the free $R$-algebra on $X$ ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]).

1. There is a unique $S$-algebra isomorphism $S\otimes_RR\langle X\rangle\to S\langle X\rangle$ with $s\otimes x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n}\mapsto s\,x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n}$ on words; its inverse sends a word to $1\otimes$ that word.
2. derivations.claim: On $V_N$, each $L_j$ is diagonal and invertible, and the $L_j$ commute. Conjugating the matrix unit $E_i:e_{i+1}\mapsto e_i$ by $L_j$ multiplies its sole nonzero entry by $q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}$; conjugating $F_i:e_i\mapsto e_{i+1}$ gives the inverse exponent. Also $K_i$ has eigenvalue $q$ on $e_i$, $q^{-1}$ on $e_{i+1}$ and $1$ on every other basis vector, so $(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $1,-1,0$ in those positions. Directly, $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $[E_i,F_i]$ is that diagonal matrix. Products $E_iE_j$ and $E_jE_i$ (and the corresponding $F$ products) both vanish when $|i-j|>1$; $E_i^2=F_i^2=0$, and each middle three-letter Serre product also vanishes because its matrix-unit indices do not compose. Thus every defining relation holds, and the quotient universal property [F1] gives the vector representation.

Define $\Delta$ on the free generators by the displayed formulas in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]]. The $\Delta(L_j)$ are mutually commuting units with the displayed inverses. Conjugation by $\Delta(L_j)$ gives the required weights on each of the two terms of $\Delta(E_i)$ and $\Delta(F_i)$, since each $K_i$ is a Laurent monomial in the commuting $L$'s. For any $i,j$, expansion gives $[\Delta(E_i),\Delta(F_j)]=[E_i,F_j]\otimes K_i+K_j^{-1}\otimes[E_i,F_j]+[E_i\otimes K_i,K_j^{-1}\otimes F_j]$. The last cross term is zero: its first product can be reordered as $q^{a_{ji}-a_{ij}}K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i=K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i$, which is its reverse product by [F3]. If $i\ne j$, the remaining terms vanish; if $i=j$, they sum to $\bigl(K_i\otimes K_i-K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\bigr)/(q-q^{-1})=\Delta\bigl((K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})\bigr)$. For $|i-j|>1$, $a_{ij}=0$ and the $K_i$ commute with $E_j,F_j$; expanding the two commutators therefore proves that the distant $E$ and $F$ relations are preserved.

Let $\gamma=q+q^{-1}$ and $S_{ij}(X,Y)=X^2Y-\gamma XYX+YX^2$ for adjacent $i,j$. For the $E$ relation write $\Delta(E_s)=A_s+B_s$ with $A_s=E_s\otimes K_s$, $B_s=1\otimes E_s$. In each of the three words $iij,iji,jii$, choose an $A$ at each selected position and a $B$ at each other position, then move the selected $K$ factors to the right using $K_rE_s=q^{a_{rs}}E_sK_r$. Grouping the resulting 24 terms by the number of selected positions gives: degree $0$ in the first factor is $1\otimes S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)$; degree $3$ is $S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)\otimes K_i^2K_j$; degree $1$ has respective coefficients $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $1+q^{-2}-\gamma q^{-1}$ on $E_i\otimes E_iE_jK_i$, $E_i\otimes E_jE_iK_i$, $E_j\otimes E_i^2K_j$; degree $2$ has respective coefficients $q^{-2}+1-\gamma q^{-1}$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$ on $E_i^2\otimes E_jK_i^2$, $E_iE_j\otimes E_iK_iK_j$, $E_jE_i\otimes E_iK_jK_i$. All six mixed coefficients are zero by the definition of $\gamma$, and the two pure terms vanish by the defining Serre relation. Thus $\Delta$ preserves every positive Serre relation.

The assignment $\phi(L_j)=L_j^{-1}$, $\phi(E_i)=F_i$, $\phi(F_i)=E_i$ preserves the presentation: it exchanges the two weight relations, sends the mixed commutator to its negative with $K_i$ replaced by $K_i^{-1}$, and exchanges the distant and Serre relations. It is an involution. On generators $\Delta(F_i)=\tau(\phi\otimes\phi)\Delta(E_i)$, where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is an algebra isomorphism. Since step 1.3 proves that the positive Serre polynomial maps to zero, applying the algebra maps $\tau$ and $\phi\otimes\phi$ proves that the negative Serre polynomial maps to zero as well. Together steps 1.2–2.1 show every relation is killed, so [F1] descends $\Delta$ to the quotient. The counit assignment kills the relations directly: each relation becomes either $1=1$ or $0=0$, so it too descends.

Both counit composites and both iterated coproduct composites are algebra homomorphisms, so it suffices by [F2] to check generators. The maps $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$ return $L_j,E_i,F_i$ from their displayed formulas. On $L_j$, both iterated coproducts give $L_j\otimes L_j\otimes L_j$; on $E_i$, both give $E_i\otimes K_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes1\otimes E_i$; on $F_i$, both give $F_i\otimes1\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i$. Hence $\Delta$ is coassociative with counit $\epsilon$. The vector representation of step 1.1 and the iterated coproduct therefore define actions on every $V_N^{\otimes n}$. They are finite sums and products of matrices with entries $0,1,q^{\pm1}$, so all entries lie in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

derivations.claim: Integral matrices. Write the iterated coproduct $E_i$ as its sum of single-position raising operators. The summand at position $j$ has coefficient $v^{h_i(w_{>j})}$; the lowering summand has coefficient $v^{-h_i(w_{<j})}$. A position cannot be used twice. For $a$ distinct raising positions, swapping two consecutive choices changes the exponent by $2$, since changing $i+1$ to $i$ increases $h_i$ by $2$. Summing the orders gives $v^{a(a-1)/2}[a]_v!$ times the coefficient using the original suffix counts: explicitly $\sum_{\pi\in S_a}v^{2\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}=v^{a(a-1)/2}[a]_v!$, as follows by inserting the largest letter, which multiplies the sum by $1+v^2+\cdots+v^{2(a-1)}$. The lowering calculation uses prefixes and the same identity. Therefore, over the generic field and then as integral matrices, $E_i^{(a)}e_w=\sum_{\substack{J\subseteq\{j:w_j=i+1\}\\|J|=a}}v^{a(a-1)/2+\sum_{j\in J}h_i(w_{>j})}e_{w(J\mapsto i)},\quad F_i^{(a)}e_w=\sum_{\substack{J\subseteq\{j:w_j=i\}\\|J|=a}}v^{a(a-1)/2-\sum_{j\in J}h_i(w_{<j})}e_{w(J\mapsto i+1)}.$ The toral generator acts on content $\alpha$ by $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_j\\t\end{smallmatrix}\right]_v$, integral by [F3]. Thus every generating matrix preserves $T$. No factorial is inverted after specialization.

Transport of the Hecke action. For $w_\mu=1^{\mu_1}\cdots N^{\mu_N}$ define $\theta_\mu(m_\mu T_d)=v^{\ell(d)}e_{w_\mu d}$. Every word of content $\mu$ occurs once, $\ell(d)=\operatorname{inv}(w_\mu d)$, and each coefficient is a unit; hence $\theta_\mu$ is an integral bijection. Standard Hecke multiplication on distinguished cosets gives an ascending swap with coefficient $1$, a descending swap with coefficient $q$ plus $(q-1)$ times the original coset, and coefficient $q$ when the two letters coincide. Multiplying the basis vectors by $v^{\operatorname{inv}(w)}$ changes the two unequal-letter swap coefficients to $v$, giving exactly the displayed tensor formula. Consequently this is an actual Hecke action, with quadratic and braid relations inherited from $H$, and $\theta=\bigoplus_\mu\theta_\mu$ is a right-module isomorphism.

Commutation can be checked locally. Put $j=i+1$. On the four two-letter words $ii,ij,ji,jj$, the nonzero local raising values are $E(ij)=ii$, $E(ji)=vii$, $E(jj)=v^{-1}ij+ji$, and the nonzero lowering values are $F(ii)=v^{-1}ij+ji$, $F(ij)=jj$, $F(ji)=vjj$. The Hecke values are $H(ii)=qii$, $H(ij)=vji$, $H(ji)=vij+(q-1)ji$, $H(jj)=qjj$. Substitution proves $EH=HE$, $FH=HF$: on $ij$ and $ji$ the raising composites give respectively $qii$ and $vqii$, and on $jj$ they give $vij+qji$; lowering gives the transposed three checks. With one active letter and one outside $\{i,j\}$ the suffix or inverse-prefix multiplier is $1$, and the outside letter has the same comparison with $i$ and $j$, so swapping or retaining that letter commutes with its replacement. With no active letter both operators are zero. Terms of the full coproduct acting outside the adjacent pair only see its total $h_i$, unchanged by its Hecke action; diagonal toral operators depend only on content. This proves commutation for $E_i,F_i,K_j$. Over the generic field divided powers commute too; since their integral matrices are given in step 1.1, their commutator entries are zero Laurent polynomials. Toral binomials commute by content. Thus $\rho$ has image in the actual integral commutant.

Orbit coordinates for that commutant. Fix source content $
u$ and split its sorted word into contiguous column blocks of lengths $
u_j$. For an $N	imes N$ nonnegative integer matrix $D=(d_{ij})$ of total $r$, with column sums $
u$ and row sums $\mu$, let $\mathcal W_D$ be the words containing exactly $d_{ij}$ letters $i$ in block $j$, and put $z_D=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W_D}v^{\operatorname{inv}_
u(w)}e_w,$ where $\operatorname{inv}_
u$ counts inversions separately inside those blocks. Within a block, pairing an ascending word and its descending swap in $yT_s=qy$ forces the descending coefficient to be $v$ times the ascending coefficient, since $v$ is a unit. Adjacent swaps connect every arrangement to the uniquely blockwise sorted word $w_D$. Hence all simultaneous $q$-eigenvectors for the source row subgroup are exactly the free span of the $z_D$, whose supports are disjoint and whose coefficient at $w_D$ is one. By the cyclic presentation [F2], evaluation at $e_{w_
u}$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_H(T_
u,T_\mu)$ with this eigenspace. Write $\xi_D$ for the map with that evaluation. These maps give an explicit integral basis, independently of any generic rank comparison, over every ring with a chosen invertible $v$.

The toral element $P_\mu=\prod_j\left[\begin{smallmatrix}K_j;0\\\mu_j\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ acts on content $\alpha$ by $\prod_j\left[\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_j\\\mu_j\end{smallmatrix}\right]_v$. If $\alpha\ne\mu$ and both sum to $r$, at least one $\alpha_j<\mu_j$, making that factor identically zero; if $\alpha=\mu$, every factor is one. Thus $\rho(P_\mu)=1_\mu$. For a diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(\mu)$ the orbit map $\xi_D$ is this projection. These conclusions remain identities at parameters where several $K_j$ eigenvalues coincide.

Define the triangular order, within fixed row and column sums, by all northeast and southwest rectangle sums $\sigma_{ab}(D)=\begin{cases}\sum_{s\le a,\ t\ge b}d_{st}&a<b,\\\sum_{s\ge a,\ t\le b}d_{st}&a>b.\end{cases}$ Write $D'\preceq D$ if every such sum is at most the corresponding sum for $D$. This is an actual partial order: differences of northeast rectangle sums recover each strictly upper entry, differences of southwest sums recover each strictly lower entry, and the fixed row sums then recover the diagonal. Put $\delta(D)=\sum_{i,j}|i-j|d_{ij}$ and $s(D)=\sum_{a\ne b}\sigma_{ab}(D)$. The diagonal-boundary sums give $\delta(D)=\sum_{a=1}^{N-1}(\sigma_{a,a+1}(D)+\sigma_{a+1,a}(D))$. Therefore $D'\prec D$ implies $\delta(D')\le\delta(D)$ and $s(D')<s(D)$. The pair $(\delta,s)$ of nonnegative integers supplies a terminating induction even when intermediate matrices have different row sums.

Extreme-column multiplication. Acting by $E_i^{(b)}$ on $z_D$ transfers $b$ letters from row $i+1$ to row $i$, distributed as $t_j$ among the column blocks, with $0\le t_j\le d_{i+1,j}$ and $\sum_jt_j=b$. Its expansion in step 4.1 has only the matrices $D+\sum_jt_j(E_{ij}-E_{i+1,j})$. Choosing the rightmost available columns greedily maximizes every suffix $\sum_{j\ge k}t_j$ and minimizes every prefix $\sum_{j\le k}t_j$. A transfer across the row boundary $i$ changes a northeast rectangle only when its row cutoff is $i$, by such a suffix; it changes a southwest rectangle only when its lower row cutoff is $i+1$, by the negative of such a prefix. Thus this greedy matrix dominates every other supported matrix in $\preceq$. For several $E_i$ executed in increasing $i$, the source row $i+1$ has not yet been changed, and each operation changes rectangle coordinates at its own boundary only. Consequently simultaneous greedy choices still give a single maximal supported matrix. If at each boundary the target row originally contains zero letters in every selected column, its coefficient is a Laurent unit: to obtain the blockwise sorted final word, all newly present $i$'s in those columns must have been raised, giving exactly one predecessor word and one subset. That predecessor is blockwise sorted, with coefficient one in $z_D$, and step 1.1 gives a single Laurent monomial. Earlier operations only depleted this target row, so its zero entries persist. Multiplying these monomials gives the claimed unit pivot, and uniqueness of successive row transfers rules out an additional path to the same final matrix.

The lower version is equally explicit. Acting by $F_i^{(b)}$ transfers letters from row $i$ to row $i+1$. Greedy selection of the leftmost available columns maximizes southwest prefix increments and minimizes northeast suffix decrements, hence gives the maximal matrix. Execute several $F_i$ in decreasing $i$; each source row is then unchanged before its turn, and the rectangle boundaries are again distinct. If all selected target entries are initially zero, the blockwise sorted final word has exactly one predecessor and chosen subset, so its coefficient is a Laurent monomial by the lowering formula of step 1.1. This proves the same maximal-support and unit-pivot assertion without invoking a Gaussian coefficient or cancelling one.

Upper elimination. Suppose $D$ has a strictly upper entry and let $k>0$ be the largest distance $j-i$ of such an entry. Set $b_i=d_{i,i+k}$ (zero when $i+k>N$) and $D_0=D-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i,i+k}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i+1,i+k},\qquad X=E_{N-1}^{(b_{N-1})}\cdots E_1^{(b_1)}.$ Zero terms with column index greater than $N$ are omitted. Thus $X$ executes its operations in increasing $i$. The rightmost nonzero column of source row $i+1$ in $D_0$ is at most $i+k$: its original distance-$k$ entry was removed, and the shifted entry from row $i$ is at $i+k$. There are at least $b_i$ letters at that column. Hence the greedy transfer selects exactly $b_i$ letters there and recovers $D$. Target row $i$ in $D_0$ has zero at column $i+k$, since that entire outer entry was removed and its added entry is at $i+k-1$. Step 7.1 therefore gives $X\xi_{D_0}=u_D\xi_D+\sum_{D'\prec D}a_{D'}\xi_{D'},\qquad u_D\in A^\times,\ a_{D'}\in A.$ Its source is still $\nu$, and its target row sum is the row sum of $D$, so these lower terms belong to that same Hom block. Also $\delta(D_0)=\delta(D)-\sum_i b_i<\delta(D)$. Every coefficient is explicitly obtained by the finite subset sums in step 1.1 and reading the blockwise sorted word coefficient of step 4.1.

Lower elimination. If $D$ is lower triangular but not diagonal, let $k>0$ be its largest lower distance and put $b_i=d_{i+1,i+1-k}$. Set $D_0=D-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i+1,i+1-k}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b_iE_{i,i+1-k},\qquad X=F_1^{(b_1)}\cdots F_{N-1}^{(b_{N-1})},$ with zero terms omitted when the column index is out of range.
